afroatlantic-ogou-feray: The comparative grid confirms how much of this is old iron in new hands: the Yoruba Ogun of the homeland is the hunter and road-opener who first cleared the paths with his blade, the blacksmith whose forge civilized the forest, the orisha who insists on being fed before any serious work begins; the Haitian Ogou keeps every one of these offices and adds the political one, because in Saint-Domingue and after, iron was the metal of the slaves — the machete that cut cane and cut masters, the chains that had to be broken, the tools that were forbidden and were seized. In the Petro register of the hot rites he appears as Ogoun Badagris, the bloody dreadful one whose voice is thunder, and in the Rada register he is the cooler soldier of the calendar saint; the two registers share a single shrine and a single ledger. For the corpus of comparative myth he supplies the Afro-Atlantic form of the culture-hero of iron: the first clearers of the road, the smiths of the social contract, the warriors whose pay is always partly owed.
afroatlantic-damballa-serpent-rainbow: In the comparative grid Damballa and Ayida stand with the world-serpents of every mythology — the Midgard serpent beneath the sea, the Chinese Yinglong and the coiling dragons of the flood-tales, the Rainbow Serpent of Australia and Melanesia — but with a Haitian particularity: the world-serpent here is not a threat to be fought but a peace to be kept. The waters that he governs are the waters of origin, and his service is a renewal of the original calm rather than a defeat of chaos; the rainbow that Ayida spans is the sign that the flood has an end. The colonial sources, seeing only the box and the oath, could not read this; the living liturgy reads it every time the paired serpents are drawn on the floor of the peristyle and the oldest drums begin to cool the air of the yard. For the comparative corpus the Haitian serpent supplies the one case in which the world-serpent is both creator and comforter, and in which the oldest god is the quietest one in the room.
afroatlantic-marassa-twins: The ritual technology of the cult is precisely calibrated to its theology: twin-plates that no single food may be served on, twin-spoons, twin-cups, two small chairs, two portions of everything, and the rule that the Marassa are fed before any other lwa — the first portion of the first dish, on the ground, with the house children standing around as if at the feeding of real children. When the twins are angry, the whole household knows it at once: the children sicken, the food spoils, the services stall, and the remedy is a double feast as quickly as it can be cooked. The Marassa therefore function as the household conscience of the religion — the lwa whose displeasure is immediate, domestic, and repairable, and whose cult teaches the primary Afro-Atlantic ethic that the doubled and the divided must be honored together. In the corpus of world myth they stand with every sacred-twin tradition, from the Ashanti twins to the Popol Vuh, supplying the Haitian case in which twinship is treated not as a heroic epoch but as a permanent domestic arrangement that must be kept in good order at every meal.
afroatlantic-gede-baron: The Gede's festival season is a study in this doubleness: on the feasts of the dead — All Souls and the days of the cemetery — the peristyle fills with black-clad, skull-faced dancers, and the services run all night, part funeral and part carnival, with the banda danced until the drums give out. The economics of the cult are equally explicit: the Gede are paid for everything — a coin for a prayer, a bottle for an audience, a substantial fee for the contract at the tomb — and they are famous for collecting; a service without payment is a service the Baron will remember. In the comparative grid they stand with every psychopomp of world mythology — Hermes, the Egyptian Anubis and Osiris, the Norse Hel — but with the Afro-Atlantic particularity that the lord of the dead is also the patron of the unborn, and that his cult is the one place in the religion where death and fertility are negotiated at the same table. For the corpus of comparative myth the Haitian Gede supply the fullest case of death as a professional service: contracted, priced, celebrated, and always, in the end, laughed with rather than at.
afroatlantic-bois-caiman: For the comparative corpus Bois Caïman supplies the Afro-Atlantic form of the covenant scene: the oath sworn over blood in the wood, the divine sanction claimed by the weakest party, and the fire that follows as the sign that the covenant has been accepted. Parallels are exact and instructive — the covenant of the Hebrew exodus, the Maccabean oath at Modin, the secret oath-societies of the Kongo and the Anjelo coast that the slave-trade carried to the Caribbean — and the Haitian case is the only one that succeeded all the way to statehood. The sensitivity of the material is proportionate to its importance: Bois Caïman is invoked by Haitians as the nation's baptism, contested by scholars as a planter's story, and claimed by the living religion as proof that the ancestors were present at the founding; the honest record keeps all three claims in view and adds none of its own. In the Motif Atlas the record anchors the cluster of oath-over-blood foundings and links the Haitian revolution to the worldwide grammar of covenant and exodus.
afroatlantic-veve-writing-gods: The pedagogy of the vèvè is worth stating plainly, because it explains why the practice survives so tenaciously: a vèvè can be learned by watching a hand draw it, without books, without literacy, without any of the institutions of writing that the colony denied the enslaved; it is a script designed by and for a population from whom reading was forbidden. The flour that carries it is food; the ash that carries it is the residue of the fire; both are humble materials, renewed every service, and the ephemerality is doctrinal — the writing belongs to the moment of contact between worlds and must not outlast it. In the comparative grid the practice stands with the ground-drawings of the Kongo, the sand-figures of West African divination (the sikidy of Madagascar, the Ifá marks of the Yoruba), and the chalk diagrams of European cunning-folk; the Haitian vèvè is the point at which all of these stream together into one liturgical art. For the Motif Atlas the record anchors the cluster of sacred sign-writing — the diviner's marks, the cosmograms, the signatures of the gods — and gives the Afro-Atlantic case in which writing itself is a rite of hospitality: the gods arrive because someone took the trouble to spell their names on the floor.
afroatlantic-bondye-grand-chemin: The Grand Chemin deserves its own close attention, because it is the image that most distinguishes this cosmology from its Old World sources. In the African homelands the worlds of the living and the dead are adjacent villages, connected by boundaries that are tended — the sacred grove, the river crossing, the family tomb inside the compound wall. In Haiti the crossing became the road: a long, dangerous, traveled distance, made by the Middle Passage and renewed by the regime of mobility that the plantation imposed — the forced march of the coffle, the flight of the maroon along the mountain paths, the constant traffic of the dead in a colony where death was everywhere at work. The road-cosmos is therefore a historical cosmology: it maps the specific geography of survival in Saint-Domingue, in which everyone, living or dead, was a traveler between two worlds, and in which every ceremony was a way-station. The Comparative value for the Motif Atlas is that this image joins the descent-myths and underworld-roads of the Greek, Sumerian, Norse and Maya traditions with an ocean-crossing account of the same structure: the road between the worlds is the Middle Passage itself, remembered cosmologically, and every ritual journey on it is at once a liturgy and a history lesson.
afroatlantic-ezili-freda: The ritual economics of her cult make the theology legible. Ezili is the most expensive of the lwa to serve: her perfumes, her white cakes, her imported lace, her pink and white candles — the altar of a rich Ezili house in Haiti is a small museum of the dream of luxury, and the poor devotee who buys one candle for her is buying, consciously, a share in the fantasy. Brown's ethnography shows the other side with equal care: in the Brooklyn apartment altar of Mama Lola, Ezili Freda's things stand beside Ezili Danto's machete and the family's Ogou flags, and the three of them constitute a single statement about love and iron and survival — the fantasy, the labor and the fight, each with its own price. In the comparative grid Ezili stands with the Aphrodite-and-Ares pair of the Greek cycle and with the Mesopotamian Inanna in her modes of desire and war; the Haitian particularity is that the pair are two names of one goddess, and that the history of slavery is written into the seam between them. For the Motif Atlas the record anchors the cluster of love-goddess-with-war-goddess and supplies the Afro-Atlantic case in which the split is explained by history rather than by theology.
